Ever wonder why some people swear “America” is a single continent, while English speakers insist it’s two?   

The answer isn’t just geography it’s a wild mix of mapmaking history, 20th-century engineering, and Cold War geopolitics.  

Here’s how America went from one giant continent to being split in two by the English-speaking world:  

1. The Single Continent Era (1507 – Late 1800s) 
In 1507, German mapmaker Martin Waldseemüller created a world map and labeled the new landmass “America” in honor of Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci. For centuries it was viewed as one continuous continent, distinct from Europe, Asia, and Africa. Even standard British and American schoolbooks taught the single-continent model well into the 19th century.  

2. The Panama Canal Split (1914) 
For a long time the only thing connecting the northern and southern landmasses was the narrow Isthmus of Panama. In 1914, the opening of the Panama Canal physically severed that connection with a permanent shipping channel. This massive engineering feat gave geographers a strong physical and psychological argument to start treating the two halves as separate entities.  

3. The Cold War Re-Write (1950s) 
The real reason the single-continent view largely vanished from English textbooks comes down to post-WWII geopolitics. Before the war, the U.S. favored isolationism and the idea of a unified “Western Hemisphere.” As America emerged as a global superpower during the Cold War, strategy shifted toward global military alliances like NATO. Around the same time, plate tectonics science showed North and South America sit on separate plates. American and British educators 👉(it all goes back to the 👑)👈 officially adopted the seven-continent model we use today.  

Where the Single Continent Still Lives... 
While English speakers use the 7-continent model, most Romance-language nations (Latin America, Spain, Portugal, Italy, etc.) still teach the traditional 6-continent model treating America as one grand, united continent.  

This historic view is why the Olympic flag has only five rings for the five inhabited continents: Europe, Asia, Africa, Oceania… and one single ring representing the entire American landmass.

🇺🇦 Fozzy Group is cutting costs following Russian attacks on its warehouses. The company is freezing hiring, canceling bonuses, and postponing salary increases, according to Forbes Ukraine.

In August alone, 10 of the group's distribution centers, which supplied "Silpo," "Fora," Fozzy, and "Thrash! Trash!," were damaged. A "Silpo" supermarket in Krivoy Rog was also destroyed, and following an attack on the night of August 28, a Fozzy hypermarket and production facilities in Vishnevoye were affected.

"We have lost part of our logistics and production infrastructure, as well as inventory. At the same time, logistics costs have increased significantly," the company reported.

Fozzy Group has canceled the planned salary review for the fall, bonuses for the third and fourth quarters, and, starting October 1, is suspending the voluntary medical insurance program and hiring for open positions.

The company stated that these measures are temporary and will be reviewed after assessing financial results and cash flow.

💬 Exclusive | End to war must serve Iran’s national interests: Deputy Parliament speaker

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Deputy Parliament Speaker Ali Nikzad has dismissed the US claim of an economic blockade on Iran as a “psychological operation,” stressing that any decision to end the war must be based on national security and interests, not pressure or war fatigue.

In an exclusive interview with IRNA on Friday, Nikzad described the US claim that Iran is under an economic blockade as part of a “psychological operation,” stressing that Iran cannot easily be isolated given its 15 neighboring countries, access to international waters and strategic position in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.
​
He said that Iran’s regional, economic and geopolitical capacities, as well as its ties with neighboring countries and Asian powers, provide significant opportunities to neutralize external pressure.
​
He added that the country’s ability to maintain its institutions and continue decision-making and governance under such conditions demonstrated Iran’s social and political capacity to preserve cohesion and rebuild its strength. External pressure, he added, does not necessarily lead to Iran’s collapse or inaction.
​
Addressing the possibility of continuing the war and the president’s remarks on ending it, Nikzad said that a distinction must be made between the “ability to continue the war” and the “wisdom of continuing it.” He stressed that the war is not an end in itself; otherwise, the ultimate objective is to safeguard national security and interests.
​
He said that the criterion for peace should not be war fatigue or economic pressure, but the outcome achieved by ending the war. If ending the war helps consolidate security, reduce economic pressure, protect national interests and secure a clear outcome from the resistance, it should be welcomed, he added.
​
Nikzad warned, however, that Iran should not be naive if the adversary seeks to use negotiations to rebuild its capabilities or impose new conditions. Negotiations and an end to the war, he said, are not the same as surrender. Iran must maintain its readiness to confront any aggression while pursuing an agreement, he added.

📲 @Irna_en​
